clinicalPearls: A benign renal epithelial tumour arising from the intercalated cells of the collecting duct
Usually discovered incidentally as a well-defined solid cortical mass
May show a central stellate scar on imaging, though this is neither sensitive nor specific
Cannot be reliably distinguished from chromophobe renal cell carcinoma by imaging alone
Renal mass biopsy can suggest the diagnosis but sampling and hybrid oncocytic tumours limit certainty
Multiple oncocytomas or oncocytosis may occur in Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome
Because malignancy cannot always be excluded preoperatively, many lesions are still resected
reference.pathophysiology: Renal oncocytoma is composed of oncocytes, cells packed with mitochondria that give an eosinophilic granular cytoplasm, and is thought to derive from the intercalated cells of the collecting duct. It is a benign neoplasm without metastatic potential, but it shares histological and immunophenotypic features with chromophobe renal cell carcinoma, which complicates diagnosis. Hybrid oncocytic-chromophobe tumours occur, particularly in the setting of Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome, reflecting overlap in their cell of origin.
additionalDifferentials: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma with eosinophilic features
Papillary renal cell carcinoma, eosinophilic type
Hybrid oncocytic tumour in Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome
additionalInvestigations: CT or MRI to characterise the solid renal mass
Renal mass biopsy where the result would change management
Immunohistochemistry to help separate it from chromophobe carcinoma
Assessment for Birt-Hogg-Dube features when tumours are multiple
Surveillance imaging when a conservative approach is chosen
redFlags: Interval growth or new symptoms suggesting the lesion is not benign
Multiple renal and cutaneous lesions suggesting a hereditary syndrome
Any histological atypia raising doubt about the benign diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Renal oncocytoma is benign with an excellent prognosis and does not metastasise; the main challenge is diagnostic certainty rather than tumour behaviour, and outcomes are excellent whether managed by surveillance or excision.
pitfalls: Relying on a central scar on imaging to diagnose it confidently
Assuming biopsy fully excludes chromophobe carcinoma
Over-treating a benign lesion or, conversely, under-treating a misclassified carcinoma
references: WHO Classification of Urinary and Male Genital Tumours
management: Renal oncocytoma is a benign, non metastasising tumour, so treatment intent is never curative oncologic the way it is for renal cell carcinoma; the main challenge is diagnostic certainty, since it cannot be reliably distinguished from chromophobe RCC or hybrid oncocytic-chromophobe tumours by imaging alone.

Work up an incidentally found renal mass with pre and post contrast CT or MRI; consider renal mass biopsy using a risk stratification approach when the result would change management, keeping in mind grading concordance is only moderate and biopsy does not always change the plan.

Immunohistochemistry can help separate oncocytoma from chromophobe RCC when biopsy is performed, though sampling limitations and hybrid tumours mean biopsy supports rather than guarantees the diagnosis.
Sestamibi SPECT/CT has been studied as an adjunct for detecting mitochondria rich tumours (chromophobe RCC and oncocytoma) but remains a research/adjunct tool rather than a required guideline step.
For lesions confidently characterised as oncocytoma, active imaging surveillance is an appropriate default, mirroring the surveillance approach used for small, localised renal masses generally.
Continue surveillance with serial cross sectional imaging roughly every 3 to 6 months, then less often once stability is demonstrated, to reassess safety over time.

Move to treatment, favouring a nephron sparing approach (partial nephrectomy) over radical nephrectomy, when malignancy cannot be confidently excluded, hybrid features are suspected, or the lesion enlarges on surveillance.

Nephron sparing surgery is preferred over radical nephrectomy whenever technically feasible because it preserves renal parenchyma and avoids the long term renal function decline associated with radical nephrectomy.

Thermal ablation and other minimally invasive options exist among small renal mass strategies (radical nephrectomy, partial nephrectomy, thermal ablation, active surveillance); involvement of an experienced urologist is essential for choosing among them.

There is no role for systemic anticancer therapy (chemotherapy, targeted agents, or immunotherapy) and no lines of therapy in the oncologic sense; the only escalation pathway is from surveillance to surgical excision if the diagnosis becomes uncertain or the lesion changes.
Radiotherapy has no established role in the management of renal oncocytoma.
After nephron sparing surgery, monitor renal function and confirm final histology, since resected specimens can occasionally reveal chromophobe RCC or a hybrid tumour on full pathologic review.

Refer to or co-manage with a urologist experienced in renal mass management for decisions between surveillance, biopsy, and surgery, especially when findings are equivocal for malignancy, and refer for genetic counselling when multiple oncocytomas or oncocytosis raise suspicion for Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome.

Refer promptly if surveillance imaging shows interval growth, new symptoms, or histological atypia that puts the benign diagnosis in doubt, since these situations may require treating the lesion as if it were renal cell carcinoma.
